--- Page 1 ---
PowerAtlas: Feasibility-Aware Language Models for
Electricity–Computing Co-Scheduling
Kaiwen Jiang1
Siya Xu1*
Ziyue Zhu1
Kaiwen Xue1
Chao Yang2
Anh Tuan Luu3
Haoran Luo3,*
1Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, China
2State Grid Liaoning Electric Power Co., Ltd., Liaoning, China
3Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
{jiangkaiwen,xusiyaxsy,zyzhu}@bupt.edu.cn
haoran.luo@ntu.edu.sg
Abstract
Electricity–computing co-scheduling (ECCS)
decides where and when computing tasks run
together with how generators are dispatched,
because task placement changes nodal demand
while power availability determines whether
tasks can be served.
Prior work addresses
such coupled problems with optimization or
learned controllers, and large language mod-
els (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate
structured decisions for scheduling and power
systems. Solver runtimes vary across instances,
and LLM outputs that parse correctly can still
violate grid and service constraints. We for-
malize ECCS as a structured decision task
and release ECBench, 2,000 instances with
Gurobi-optimal reference schedules and exe-
cutable checks for grid limits, task service, cost,
and latency. We propose PowerAtlas, which
trains an LLM with supervised initialization
and Feasibility-Aware GRPO on deterministic
scorer feedback, and generates the joint sched-
ule in a single response without solver calls or
retrieval. On 10–40 paired instances per back-
bone, selected PowerAtlas checkpoints lower
violations by 89–98% and penalized cost by up
to 26× relative to base models, with residual
supply deficits. Code and data are available
online.1
1
Introduction
Electricity–Computing Co-Scheduling (ECCS)
jointly schedules computing tasks and power dis-
patch: task placement changes nodal demand,
while power availability determines whether place-
ments can be served (Figure 1). Growing AI work-
loads increase data-center electricity demand (In-
ternational Energy Agency, 2025). Shifting jobs
across times and sites (Lindberg et al., 2021, 2022;
Wiesner et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2026; Zhang
et al., 2024; Shahout et al., 2025) offers flexibility,

grid constraints to joint dispatch and placement. Deter-
ministic format, grid, and task-service checks assess can-
didate schedules; actions and outcomes are schematic.
subject to available grid capacity and prices (Wang
et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
Prior
co-scheduling
research
coordinates
this flexibility through optimization and learn-
ing (Zhang et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2025; Wan and
Li, 2026; Fan and Zhao, 2026; Liu et al., 2026;
Luo et al., 2025c), building on unit commitment,
dispatch, and power-flow models (Chen et al.,
2022; Aharwar et al., 2023; Wuijts et al., 2024;
Fu et al., 2021; Kunya et al., 2023; Xu et al.,
2023; Zhao et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Taheri
and Molzahn, 2024; Barrows et al., 2019). More
recently, LLMs (Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al.,
2024; Technology Innovation Institute, 2024) have
supported reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al.,
2023b), optimization (Huang et al., 2025; Yang
et al., 2024; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024), and
power-system applications (Mohammadi et al.,
2025; Bernier et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Jia
et al., 2025; Jadhav et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024).
Two challenges remain (Figure 2). Coupled op-
timization can incur variable solve times, whereas
fast LLM outputs can be syntactically valid yet
violate grid or service constraints. Learning a re-

Figure 2: ECCS motivation and PowerAtlas overview. (a–b) Grid constraints and task/data sources define the
problem. (c–d) Optimization latency and constraint-violating LLM outputs motivate (e) learning joint dispatch and
placement from domain knowledge and training feedback.
sponse schema alone does not resolve these de-
pendencies. We therefore ask whether verifiable
training feedback can improve direct generation of
jointly admissible schedules.
We formulate ECCS as a structured decision task
and introduce ECBench, with 2,000 calibrated in-
stances, Gurobi-optimal reference schedules, and
executable metrics for grid constraints, service,
cost, and latency. Our method, PowerAtlas, com-
bines supervised initialization with Feasibility-
Aware Policy Alignment. Domain knowledge
and deterministic scoring support training; infer-
ence produces one joint schedule without retrieval,
solver calls, or repair at decision time.
Across three open-weight backbones, paired
comparisons on 10–40 instances show 89–98%
lower mean violation and up to 26× lower penal-
ized cost. Archived stage comparisons characterize
initialization and alignment in output completeness
and scheduling quality. We further analyze residual
supply deficits, checkpoint sensitivity, and service
trade-offs; Section 6.1 specifies the sampling and
satisfaction conventions for these comparisons.
2
Related Work
Electricity-Computing Co-Scheduling. Work-
load shifting reduces costs (Radovanovi´c et al.,
2023; Wiesner et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2026;
Nkwawir et al., 2025). Prior formulations combine
grid signals (Zhang et al., 2022; Williams et al.,
2026) with hierarchical, spatial, thermal, or multi-
energy constraints (Han et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025;
Ali and Özkasap, 2024; Liu, 2024; Bian et al., 2024)
and optimization or reinforcement learning (Luo
et al., 2025c; Qi et al., 2022). ECBench evaluates
learned policies on coupled instances.
LLM-Driven Scheduling and Optimization.
LLM optimization (Abgaryan et al., 2024; Xiao
et al., 2024) draws on retrieval (Luo et al., 2024,
2025a,b, 2026), reasoning and tools (Wei et al.,
2022; Yao et al., 2023b; Schick et al., 2023; Yao
et al., 2023a; Shinn et al., 2023), and reinforcement
learning with verification (Ouyang et al., 2022;
Schulman et al., 2017; Lightman et al., 2024; Guo
et al., 2025). Power applications include schedul-
ing (Mongaillard et al., 2024), dispatch (Moham-
madi et al., 2025; Bernier et al., 2025; Yang et al.,
2026; Jia et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Sarwar
et al., 2025), security (Ruan et al., 2024), bench-
marks (Zhou et al., 2024; Han et al., 2022), topol-
ogy modeling (Chen et al., 2025), and physical
verification (Jiang et al., 2026). PowerAtlas tar-
gets direct joint scheduling with executable training
feedback on the generated dispatch and placement.
3
Task Definition
ECCS generates joint power dispatch and task
placement to minimize operating cost under grid
and service constraints. Format validity and physi-
cal feasibility are separate requirements (Figure 3).
The input S = (SC, ST , SK, SF ) specifies grid
constraints, task requirements, domain knowledge,

Figure 3: PowerAtlas decision interface. The policy maps S = (SC, ST , SK, SF ) to one response containing the
joint decision D = (DP , DC). Nodal demand couples 24-hour power dispatch with task placement across four data
centers. Reported inference uses neither solver calls nor retrieval.
and the output schema. Figure 3 separates these
components: SC describes the grid, ST the task
attributes, SK dispatch rules and scheduling guid-
ance, and SF the response contract. Grid con-
straints include DC power flow, line and gener-
ator limits, ramping, and minimum up/down times.
RTS-GMLC (Barrows et al., 2019) has 73 buses,
120 lines, and 73 thermal units: 6 are agent-
controlled and 67 follow economic dispatch. The
37 tasks specify priority, time windows, rack and
power demand, duration, drop penalties, and mi-
gratability across data-center locations.
The decision D
= (DP , DC) contains 24-
hour schedules for five non-swing units, expressed
as off or percentages in [0, 100] mapped to
[Pmin, Pmax]. The evaluator re-optimizes the swing
unit within its capacity. Each task is assigned drop
or (dc, start) across four data centers, each with 11
racks and idle power Pidle = 0.25 Pmax. Placement
changes nodal demand and dispatch feasibility; Ap-
pendix F.1 specifies incomplete-output handling.
Let C(D; S) include generation, lost-load, drop,
and migration costs, and F(S) collect the grid and
service constraints. The oracle solves
D⋆= arg
min
D∈F(S) C(D; S).
(1)
PowerAtlas approximates this optimization with a
policy πθ parameterized by θ,
D = πθ(S),
(2)
The policy is trained to reduce violations and cost,
but does not guarantee D ∈F(S). The hourly
evaluator does not check ramping, minimum up/-
down times, or reserve; its scores therefore do not
certify full ECCS feasibility. Section 5 gives the
training objective and schedule-level rewards.
4
Benchmark: ECBench
ECBench provides training instances, optimal ref-
erence schedules, and executable evaluation of
structured LLM decisions under coupled grid
and task-service constraints.
4.1
Dataset Construction
Figure 4 summarizes ECBench construction. RTS-
GMLC documentation, data-center records, and
LLM-assisted generation yield 2,000 instances
from 50 days, 4 load levels, and 10 seeds (Table 5).
Rack count and peak-load normalization are cali-
brated from a real facility; task attributes are syn-
thetic, with relaxed scheduling restrictions.
A joint unit-commitment and DC power-flow
MILP models task placement, reserve, data-center
capacity, and nodal balance (Appendix D.1).
Gurobi (Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2024) solves
it to optimality in 16.8 s at the median, 35.9 s at the
95th percentile, and up to 148.1 s. Deterministic
power-flow and balance checks validate instance–
solution pairs. The seed split contains 1,600 train-
ing and 400 test instances. The retrieval corpus
contains 520 solved training cases and 31 expert
notes, for 551 entries; test cases are excluded (Ap-
pendix D.2). The seed-based split shares operat-
ing regimes; Appendix F.1 specifies reporting-pool
membership and checkpoint selection.

4.2
Benchmark Design
A deterministic evaluator scores each test instance
with the agent’s dispatch fixed. For each hour t of
the horizon T = 24, it solves a nodal DC power-
flow feasibility linear program (LP) over the bus set
N and line set L. The LP minimizes the lost-load,
over-generation, and line-overload slacks p↓
n,t, p↑
n,t,
and f+
ℓ,t. These slacks and the submitted decision
determine four groups of metrics.
The violation score (Viol, in MWh-equivalent
units; lower is better) combines grid slacks and
task-capacity excesses. Hourly slacks in MW are
accumulated over the 24-hour horizon,
Vgrid = P
n,t(p↓
n,t + p↑
n,t) + P
ℓ,t f+
ℓ,t,
Viol = Vgrid + Violtask.
(3)
where Vgrid sums the three grid slacks over all
buses or lines and t = 1, . . . , T, and Violtask
is the MWh-equivalent task violation.
Viol is
averaged over evaluated instances.
Computing
satisfaction credits tasks P under two conven-
tions. Placement-only scores count retained as-
signments. Grid-aware scores additionally exclude
task-specific violations and unpowered hours; nei-
ther convention certifies all capacity constraints
(Appendix D.3).
For n tasks with value vi,
rack demand ri, and duration di:
S-cnt = 100 |P|

The three rates measure task count, value, and rack-
hours. S-H/M/L give the rates for each priority
tier. Cost combines generation, grid-slack penal-
ties, task dropping, and migration:
Cost = Cgen+Cmig+P
i∈D vi+CLOLVgrid, (5)
where Cgen is generation cost, CLOL is the com-
mon grid-slack penalty rate, D is the submit-
ted drop set, and Cmig is migration cost.
The
evaluator prices all three grid slacks at this
rate; the oracle objective prices lost load (Ap-
pendix D.1). Re-scored cost fixes minimum-slack
ties by minimizing swing output (Appendix F.7).
Latency reports mean wall-clock decision time
under each model’s serving conditions, without
dispersion estimates. Appendix D.3 details the
evaluator’s constraint coverage.
5
Methodology: PowerAtlas
Algorithm 1 summarizes policy training using the
reference schedules constructed in Figure 4. Pow-
erAtlas learns the output schema and scheduling
patterns through supervised initialization, then re-
fines the policy with feasibility-aware policy align-
ment using domain-specific rewards. The available
training scorer checks tasks and aggregate power
balance; final evaluation uses a nodal DC LP. These
procedures have different constraint coverage (Ap-
pendix D.3). Neither feeds corrections back to the
model at inference during schedule generation.
5.1
Structured Decision Generation
For each instance, the policy πθ maps the input
specification S to a joint decision through the inter-
face in Figure 3. The structured prompt combines
hourly grid signals (load, renewable generation,
net load, and aggregate fixed generation), task at-
tributes, domain guidance, and the output contract.


--- Page 5 ---
The decision D = (DP , DC) is emitted in one re-
sponse. The policy πθ decodes it autoregressively
as a templated token sequence y,
πθ(D | S) =

The response contains a <reason> rationale (Wei
et al., 2022) and an <answer> block: TASKS as-
signs drop or (dc, start); POWER gives 24 values
per adjustable unit. Training may retrieve cases
through Graph-R1 (Luo et al., 2026, 2025a); re-
ported inference uses no retrieval.
5.2
Feasibility-Aware Policy Alignment
Full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on solved
instances (S, D⋆) minimizes response-token cross-
entropy for the target y⋆,
LSFT(θ) = −E(S,D⋆)

Only response tokens contribute to the loss; the

Feasibility-aware policy alignment assigns a
terminal reward R(τ) to the completed response
τ = y1:|y| and maximizes Eτ∼πθ[R(τ)]. The token-
level state is (S, y<k) and the action is the next
token yk. For each instance q, the behavior policy
πθold samples N trajectories {τi}N
i=1. We optimize
a critic-free, group-relative objective in the style of
GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), replacing the value net-
work of PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) with a group
baseline. Following Graph-R1 (Luo et al., 2026)
and reinforcement-learning alignment of reasoning
LLMs (Ouyang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025), we
use the objective

6
Experiments
We evaluate PowerAtlas on ECBench through four
research questions (Tables 1–3, Figures 5 and 7):
RQ1, can verifier-guided training improve con-
straint satisfaction in generated schedules; RQ2,
what do supervised initialization and feasibility-
aware alignment each contribute; RQ3, which con-
straint violations persist after training; and RQ4,
how do performance and service trade-offs vary
across checkpoints and operating conditions?
6.1
Experimental Setup
ECBench contains 2,000 instances with Gurobi-
optimal reference schedules. The retrieval corpus
uses only the training split. Eight frontier LLMs
(Table 1) use the same prompt through an OpenAI-
compatible API; three untrained open-weight back-
bones provide baselines before domain training.
Supervised initialization is followed by up to 60
alignment steps. Reported inference uses greedy
decoding in one response, without retrieval or a
solver. Main tables use grid-aware satisfaction;
placement-only training diagnostics are separately
identified in Figure 5 and Appendix F.1. Missing
units or hours are treated as offline. Latency in-
cludes the serving path: remote APIs for frontier
models and local vLLM for open-weight models.
Frontier results cover repeated runs on one shared
high-load instance. Open-weight baselines cover
10, 12, or 40 instances; trained checkpoints use a
40-instance pool also used for selection. Table 2
pairs identical IDs within each backbone; these
retrospective comparisons are not blind test results.

6.3
Contributions of Initialization and
Alignment (RQ2)
Supervised initialization. Table 3 separates two
archived SFT outputs:
the earlier archive has
9,084.2 MWh mean violation, while SFT-16 has
682.4 MWh and 43.6% grid-aware value satisfac-
tion. Their initialization histories must not be con-
flated.
Feasibility-aware alignment. Relative to the
SFT-16 archive, PowerAtlas has 68.3% lower mean
violation, about 2.1× lower cost, and 65.2% grid-
aware value satisfaction on identical instances. The
no-initialization archive remains at 10,730.2 MWh.

6.4
Residual Constraint Violations (RQ3)
Dispatch and service failures. Untrained Falcon3-
3B produces usable dispatches on 3/40 instances.
Figure 7 illustrates incomplete dispatch, supply
deficits, capacity overflow, and violations of task
deadlines or migration rules.
Residual violations. Training lowers violation
six- to fifty-fold and improves load following (Fig-
ure 5(a)–(b)). Falcon3-3B’s mean/median violation
is 216.6/75.5 MWh: lost load contributes 73%,
over-generation 8%, line overload 1%, and task
violations 17% (rounded). Supply deficits dom-

Penalties and feasibility. Lost-load penalties
account for 65–99% of baseline costs and 50–66%
after training. Remaining cost gaps reflect physical
deficits and task coverage. No selected backbone
has a strictly valid output passing all hourly grid/-
task checks among its 40 cases (Appendix F.7);
mean improvements do not imply complete feasi-
bility.
6.5
Checkpoint and Operating-Condition
Sensitivity (RQ4)
Checkpoint sensitivity. In a separate archived
run, initialization raises Falcon3-3B’s placement
value satisfaction from 6.8 to 91.6 without mate-
rially changing the median training-side balance
residual; alignment halves the residual (Figure 5(c);
Appendix F.4). Satisfaction peaks at 93.9 at step
40, versus 91.5 at step 60 (panel (d)); selection and
reporting share one pool.
Operating conditions. Trained value satisfac-
tion spans 89.8–97.3 across sampled loads and
seasons, versus below 25% before training (Fig-
ure 5(e)).
These results characterize variation
within shared training/reporting dates and load
regimes. Transfer to unseen conditions, topologies,
or horizons remains to be evaluated using held-out
regimes and independent checkpoint selection.
Service trade-offs. In the paired Qwen sub-
set, grid-aware value satisfaction is 79.0%, but
low-priority service is 3.1% versus 91.8% for high-
priority tasks. The corresponding low-priority rates
are 68.3% for Llama and 66.9% for Falcon (Ta-
ble 2). These tier-specific outcomes complement
aggregate value satisfaction.
7
Conclusion
PowerAtlas studies verifier-guided structured gen-
eration for electricity–computing co-scheduling us-
ing ECBench, with 2,000 instances and solved ref-
erences. On identical archived instances for each
backbone, selected checkpoints reduce mean vi-
olation by 89–98% and penalized cost by up to
26× relative to base models. Stage comparisons
use unified grid-aware scoring. Residual physical
violations and strict-output failures remain: these
results demonstrate improved retrospective scores,
while independent testing and complete schedule
verification remain necessary for establishing reli-
able co-scheduling performance.


--- Page 9 ---
Limitations
Reported gains across three backbones do not
establish consistent feasibility: Falcon3-3B re-
tains 216.6 MWh mean violation, largely unserved
load. Shared operating regimes, checkpoint se-
lection, and incomplete configuration provenance
also limit generalization claims.
Future research will evaluate all methods on the
full test set with consistent metrics and independent
checkpoint selection. It will test held-out operating
regimes and compare solver and retrieval baselines
under matched settings and latency budgets.
Ethics Statement
The reported experiments evaluate electricity–
computing co-scheduling in a modeled benchmark.
Generated schedules can violate grid limits or leave
computing tasks without power, even when aggre-
gate scores improve. Operational use would re-
quire independent feasibility checks, human over-
sight, and safe fallback procedures; the reported re-
sults do not establish deployment readiness. Value-
weighted scheduling can also disadvantage low-
priority tasks. Evaluation should therefore report
service outcomes across priority tiers, rather than
rely only on aggregate value or cost.
ECBench combines a power-system test model
with synthetic computing tasks calibrated from fa-
cility records. Sharing and reuse of research arti-
facts should protect sensitive facility information
and respect the licenses and access conditions of
source data and model backbones.
The public
repository supports research transparency; bench-
mark results should not be interpreted as guaran-
tees of safety, fairness, or reliability in operational
settings.
Acknowledgments
This work was supported by the Fundamental Re-
search Funds for the Beijing University of Posts
and Telecommunications (Grant 2025TSQY03).
We thank a provincial electric power company in
China for jointly building the experimental network
and providing scoped data-center access without
disclosing security-sensitive operational data.

A
Prompts Used in PowerAtlas
PowerAtlas serializes each instance into a structured prompt and generates the joint decision as one
templated response. Figure 8 presents the scheduling interface (a), retrieval query (b), and an illustrative
supervised target (c). The verifier and reward computation are given in Appendix C. These templates
describe the interface, rather than verbatim transcripts of every historical run. Placeholders in {curly
braces} are filled per instance using the corresponding grid and task specification.
(a)
ECCS Scheduling Prompt
[SYSTEM]
You are an electricity-computing co-scheduling agent. Given a 24-hour power-system state and a
list of computing tasks, output a single schedule that (1) respects power balance, DC power-flow,
and line-capacity limits; (2) honors per-data-center power capacity and each task's release,
deadline, and tier; and (3) minimizes total operating cost. First reason inside <reason>...
</reason>, then output ONLY the decision inside <answer>...</answer>.
[USER]
Grid: RTS-GMLC, {n_bus} buses, {n_line} lines, {n_unit} thermal units.
Controllable generators (the swing unit absorbs the residual): {unit_table}
Hourly signal h=1..24: load / renewable / net_load / fixed_gen = {profiles}
Data centers: {n_dc} DCs, each with capacity C={C} racks, peak power {Pmax_dc} MW,
idle power {Pidle} MW.
Tasks (one row each):
id | origin_dc | release | deadline | duration | demand | power | migratable |
priority | drop_penalty | mig_cost
{task_rows}
Retrieved solved cases (optional priors): {retrieved_cases}
CONSTRAINTS
- a placed task starts within [release, deadline - duration + 1];
- a non-migratable task runs at its origin DC; a migratable one may run at any DC;
- at every DC and hour: active rack-demand <= C, and DC load (idle + task power)
<= DC peak power;
- generation (fixed + controllable + swing) must cover the grid background plus all
data-center power, and each controllable unit must stay within [Pmin, Pmax].
(task 'demand' = number of racks; task 'power' = MW draw.)
[OUTPUT FORMAT]
<reason> ... </reason>
<answer>
TASKS: <per task>
drop
|
(dc=<id>, start=<hour>)
POWER: <per controllable unit>
24 hourly levels, each 'off' or a number in [0,100]
meaning percent between Pmin and Pmax
</answer>
(b)
Knowledge Retrieval Query
[RETRIEVAL QUERY]
Season={season}; peak_load={peak}; renewable_share={rshare}; congestion={congested_lines};
task_mix={tier_histogram}; horizon=24h.
Return the top-{k} training instances whose (grid regime, task profile) are most similar, each
with its Gurobi-optimal TASKS/POWER decision as an in-context prior.
(c)
Supervised Initialization Target
<reason>
Peak net load at h=18; lines {L12,L27} near limit => pre-commit units {g2,g5};
defer low-tier tasks {t7,t9} to off-peak; place high-tier tasks {t1,t3} at release.
</reason>
<answer>
TASKS: t1 (dc=2, start=9); t2 drop; t3 (dc=1, start=14); ...
POWER: g1 [p1..p24]; g2 [p1..p24]; ...; g5 [p1..p24]
# percent of Pmin..Pmax
</answer>
Figure 8: PowerAtlas interface templates: instance serialization and output contract (a), a retrieval query (b), and an
illustrative supervised target (c). Retrieval is used during training only.
A.1
ECCS Scheduling Prompt
The agent receives the grid signal, the task list, and
(optionally) retrieved solved cases, and must emit
a two-block decision: one line per task and one
24-point trajectory per agent-controlled unit. The
verifier scores only the content of <answer>.
Supervised target.
During supervised initializa-
tion, the policy is trained to reproduce the tem-
plated serialization of the oracle decision D⋆. The
<reason> field is a short rationale distilled from the
solved instance, while the verifier evaluates only
the <answer> block.


--- Page 14 ---
A.2
Knowledge Retrieval Prompt
Solved training cases are retrieved with the hy-
pergraph retriever of Graph-R1 (Luo et al., 2026,
2025a); the query encodes the instance’s grid
regime and task profile so that priors match the
current state.
B
Theoretical Proof
We establish three properties of the reward, group-
relative update, and hourly evaluator. Each follows
from the stated equations under explicit assump-
tions. The statements concern the scoring equations
and evaluator under these assumptions.
B.1
Proof of Proposition 1
Proposition 1.
Suppose κ, ϕ, sval, scnt ∈[0, 1],
the weights are nonnegative with ηv + ηc = wc +
wp = 1, and c⋆
tr ≥0, λtr ≥0.
Wherever
ctr
θ + λtrVtr > 0, the well-formed base reward in
Equations (11)–(14) lies in [0, 1]. With cost, refer-
ence cost, and task-quality terms fixed, this reward
is nonincreasing in Vtr.
Proof.
The retained-value/count mixture is a con-
vex combination of two numbers in [0, 1]. Multi-
plication by κϕ ∈[0, 1] preserves that interval, so
Qcompute ∈[0, 1]. The grid ratio is nonnegative,
and clipping it above at one gives Qgrid ∈[0, 1].
Their convex combination therefore lies in [0, 1].
For V2 ≥V1 with positive denominators,
c⋆

Taking the minimum with one preserves this order-
ing, as does multiplication by wp ≥0 and addition
of the fixed computing term. On the unsaturated

(16)
The malformed-output reward is −r0 < 0, below
every well-formed base reward.
□
Consequence.
The power term penalizes larger
training residuals when the other terms are held
fixed. Across different schedules, cost and task
quality can also change, so a larger total reward
need not imply a smaller violation. The bound
applies to the base reward; the available implemen-
tation’s capped retrieval bonus is documented in
Appendix C.
B.2
Proof of Proposition 2
Proposition 2.
For a group of N ≥2 finite re-
wards, let ¯R be their mean, sR their standard devi-
ation, and δ > 0. The advantages in Equation (10)
sum to zero. If all rewards are identical, every
advantage is zero and the reward-driven clipped
surrogate in Equation (8) contributes no policy gra-
dient for that group.
Proof.
All advantages have the same positive de-
nominator. Thus
N
X
i=1
ˆAi =
P
i Ri −N ¯R
sR + δ
= 0.
(17)
If Ri = r for every i, then ¯R = r, sR = 0, and
every numerator vanishes. Treating sampled re-
wards and advantages as fixed during the policy
update, both arguments of the clipped minimum
are then zero for every token and every policy ratio.
Their contribution and its gradient are zero. The
KL regularizer is separate and may still contribute
a gradient.
□
Consequence.
A group consisting entirely of
malformed outputs receives the same −r0 penalty
and supplies no relative reward signal. This ex-
plains the role of supervised initialization in obtain-
ing parseable trajectories before alignment.
B.3
Proof of Proposition 3
Proposition 3.
Assume the hourly LP in Equa-
tion (30) is feasible and attains its finite optimum.
Its optimal objective is zero if and only if its
fixed dispatch and task-induced loads admit a so-
lution with zero lost-load, over-generation, and
line-overload slacks, using the evaluator’s allowed
swing dispatch and renewable curtailment. Zero
objectives at every hour do not certify all intertem-
poral ECCS constraints.
Proof.
The objective is the sum of nonnegative
slacks with strictly positive unit coefficients. A
zero optimum therefore requires every slack in
an optimal solution to be zero. Conversely, any
feasible solution with all those slacks zero attains
objective zero, which is globally minimal by non-
negativity. For the second statement, consider an
illustrative two-hour, single-bus system with a fixed
non-swing generator, output bounds [0, 100] MW,
an upward ramp limit of 10 MW/h, and no renew-
able or swing contribution. Set dispatch and de-
mand to 20 MW in hour one and 80 MW in hour
two. Each hourly balance is exact and there are

Algorithm 2 PowerAtlas Training and Evaluation
Workflow
Input: Solved training instances Dtrain; pretrained policy;
reporting pool E; training configuration.
Output: Trained policy and metrics for its generated deci-
sions.
1: Serialize training instances and oracle targets using Ap-
pendix A.
2: Build the retrieval index from training cases and expert
notes (Appendix D.2).
3: Run supervised initialization with Equation (7); freeze the
resulting reference policy.
4: for each configured alignment step do
5:
Sample an instance batch and N trajectories per in-
stance, with training-time retrieval where enabled.
6:
Parse answers and compute training rewards; record
the scorer version, penalty, and any retrieval bonus.
7:
Compute group-relative advantages using Equa-
tion (10).
8:
Update with the clipped objective and KL regulariza-
tion in Equation (8).
9: end for
10: Select the checkpoint under the reported protocol (Ap-
pendix F.1).
11: for each instance in E do
12:
Generate one greedy response without retrieval, solver
calls, or repair.
13:
Parse the joint task and power decision.
14:
Apply task checks and the hourly nodal LP to the
submitted decision; record metrics and latency.
15: end for
no lines to overload, so both hourly objectives are
zero. However, the 60 MW increase exceeds the
ramp limit. Thus hourly feasibility does not imply
feasibility of the joint two-hour schedule.
□
Consequence.
The evaluator certifies only the
constraints it includes, with the swing unit re-
optimized at each hour.
Ramping, commit-
ment, and task legality require their corresponding
checks; coverage is listed in Appendix D.3. A zero
hourly grid objective should not be interpreted as a
guarantee of complete ECCS feasibility.
C
PowerAtlas Algorithm Details
Algorithm 2 connects dataset preparation, the two
training stages, and evaluation. Algorithm 1 gives
the group-relative update itself. Retrieval is avail-
able in training rollouts, while reported inference
generates one joint decision without retrieved ex-
amples, solver calls, or repair.
Output parsing and reward.
The training scorer
parses the <answer> block and computes task qual-
ity and a power score. Its available implementation
uses aggregate balance rather than the hourly nodal
DC LP employed for final evaluation. Section 5.2
defines the base reward; malformed outputs receive
−r0. The count weight ηc reduces the incentive to

Q_compute = retained * coverage * (1 if task_checks_pass

# --- training-side power score (not the final nodal LP)

Q_grid
= min(1, c_train_ref/(c_train_policy +

---------------------------------------------------
reward = w_c * Q_compute + w_p * Q_grid

reconciliation.

courages leaving demand uncovered. Run-specific
settings and retrieval bonuses are discussed in Ap-
pendix C.
Complexity Analysis.
Let B be the number of
instances in a training batch, N the trajectories
per instance, Troll the cost of generating one trajec-
tory, and Tscore its scoring cost. The batch requires
BN rollouts and scorer calls; their serial work is
proportional to BN(Troll + Tscore), in addition to
retrieval and the policy update. Parallel serving
changes wall-clock time without changing these
counts. Table 4 specifies the group size and genera-
tion budgets. At inference, the policy generates one
response. The separate evaluator solves H = 24
hourly feasibility programs and applies task checks
after generation. The one-response interface avoids
repeated policy–solver interaction. Wall-clock la-
tency depends on hardware, response length, and
serving conditions.
Hyperparameters.
Table 4 records the reported
settings for the three backbones, with model-
specific exceptions shown explicitly.
Full-
parameter supervised initialization is followed by
critic-free policy alignment with vLLM rollouts.
Inference uses greedy autoregressive decoding in
one response, without a solver.
Training rollouts may interleave retrieval and
generation for up to 8 turns, returning the top-5
entries per retrieval with a total response budget
of 4,096 tokens. Tool calls within a turn run in
parallel. With N = 2 trajectories and batches of 8
instances, training fits on two GPUs. Each group-
relative advantage is therefore based on only one
pair of rewards. Identical rewards yield zero rel-

Implementation provenance.
The available fast
scorer sets λtr = 3,000 $/MWh, whereas the nomi-
nal configuration previously reported 9,000. It also
adds 0.1 min(nsearch, 2) to the base reward for a
well-formed output. The retained code snapshot
does not identify the scorer configuration and roll-
out sampling settings for each historical checkpoint.
Table 4 records the reported settings; greedy decod-
ing refers to inference.

policy parameter offloading.

ECBench Detail
This appendix expands Section 4.2 into a self-

D.1
Task Design

description ST , domain knowledge SK, and the
output-format contract SF (Figure 3). Retrieval
augments training only; reported inference con-
tains no retrieved cases (Appendix D.2). Table 5
summarizes the key parameters.

n,t ≥0 the lost load at bus n (priced at CLOL
in the objective), γ = 0.03 the spinning-reserve
margin, rk the rack demand of task k and C the
rack capacity of a data center. Minimum up- and
down-time constraints on ug,t are enforced in the
solved program in the usual big-M form and are
omitted here; the oracle formulation includes them.
The hourly evaluator’s constraint coverage is speci-
fied in Appendix D.3. The oracle permits penalized
lost load, so solver optimality does not itself imply
zero unmet demand.
Two evaluator conventions affect the reported
metrics. First, the MWh-equivalent Violtask in
Equation (3) converts task-side hard violations
into power. For each (data center, hour) cell with
rack demand above capacity C, excess racks are
converted using the per-rack power draw.
For
cells with total draw above Qd, excess megawatts
are counted directly. Window, migratability, and
invalid-placement violations add no MW term but
exclude the task from satisfaction scores.
Sec-
ond, the migration term of (18) is πkmk with
mk ∈{0, 1} indicating that task k runs outside
ok and πk = 8 rk its price in the released cost con-
figuration. Migration charges are proportional to
the number of racks moved. The program is solved
to optimality with Gurobi (Gurobi Optimization,
LLC, 2024) to obtain D⋆and the reference cost c⋆.
D.2
Benchmark Construction
Each ECBench instance couples a power-system
model with a data-center workload and is paired
with an oracle-optimal decision. (i) Grid side. We
build on the RTS-GMLC test system (Barrows
et al., 2019) (73 buses, 120 transmission lines, and
73 thermal units, of which 6 are agent-controlled
and 67 follow economic dispatch), and evaluate
all combinations of 50 representative days span-
ning all twelve months, four data-center load levels
ρ ∈{1, 2, 4, 6}%, and 10 random seeds, to ob-
tain hourly profiles of load, renewable generation,
net load, and aggregate fixed generation over a
24-hour horizon. One of the six controlled units
is the swing unit, which absorbs residual imbal-
ance. (ii) Computing side. Each instance con-
tains 37 synthetic computing tasks calibrated from
data-center records, each with a priority tier (high-
/medium/low), a release time, a deadline, a value,


--- Page 18 ---
and a drop penalty. Task power ranges over 1.4–
33.5 MW and duration over 2–6 hours, and the
tier mix across the 74,000 tasks of the benchmark
is 50.8% high, 21.9% medium, 27.3% low. (iii)
Coupling. Nodal power balance, DC power-flow
and line-capacity limits, and per-data-center power
capacity link the two domains: task placement
changes nodal demand, and the grid state constrains
admissible placements. (iv) Oracle labels. Ev-
ery instance is solved to optimality by the Gurobi
MILP solver (Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2024),
yielding the reference decision D⋆and reference
cost c⋆used for both supervised initialization and
reward normalization. We generate 2,000 instances
and split them by random seed into 1,600 training
and 400 test instances. The splits share operating
regimes, while the retrieval corpus uses only train-
ing instances. Checkpoint selection and reporting-
pool membership are specified in Appendix F.1.
Retrieval corpus.
The corpus contains 551 en-
tries: 520 solved ECCS instances with grid regimes,
task profiles, and Gurobi-optimal schedules, plus
31 expert notes on scheduling and data-center en-
ergy use. All cases come from the 1,600-instance
training split. Entries are indexed using the Graph-
R1 hypergraph retriever (Luo et al., 2026, 2025a).
Retrieval is used during training; reported infer-
ence runs contain no retrieved cases in SK when
generating a joint schedule.
D.3
Evaluation Metric Design
Hourly feasibility program.
The evaluator com-
putes Viol independently of the model’s stated cal-
culations. For each hour t, it fixes the dispatch of
the five non-swing controlled units and the data-
center load implied by task placements, then solves
the nodal DC feasibility LP

with all slacks non-negative, where νn,t is the nodal
injection, Rn,t the available renewable at bus n and
cn,t its curtailment, and p↓, p↑and f+ are the lost-
load, over-generation and line-overload slacks of
Section 4.2. The evaluator re-optimizes the swing
unit rather than using a model-specified dispatch.
Its capacity limits determine how much imbalance
it can absorb. Summing the three types of slack
over 24 hours gives the grid contribution to Viol;
task violations are added as in Equation (3). The
same LP supplies Figure 5(b). Non-negative slacks
permit scoring schedules with unmet demand or
line overloads. These hourly checks do not certify
full intertemporal feasibility.
The evaluator of Section 4.2 reports violations
and penalized cost. Viol combines grid slacks with
task-capacity penalties in MWh-equivalent units;
S-cnt/S-val/S-rh are the credited fractions of task
count, penalty-weighted value, and rack-hours un-
der the specified convention; S-H/S-M/S-L are
tier-wise satisfaction rates; Cost is operating cost
plus grid-slack penalties in dollars; and Latency
is the wall-clock decision time, from submitting
the prompt to a parsed decision containing the joint
schedule.
Metric definitions. Let K be the tasks of an in-
stance and Ksrv ⊆K the tasks credited by the
grid-aware scorer (retained, without a task-specific
violation flag, and outside unpowered hours), and
let vk, rk and dk be the value, rack demand and
duration of task k. Grid violation is Equation (3),
and the three satisfaction rates are

gration and drop penalties, and all three grid slacks
priced at CLOL (Equation (5)), and Latency is the
end-to-end decision time. These definitions match
the evaluator of Section 4.2.

Output-range handling is not a separate test of
raw numeric compliance: the final parser clips
numeric percentages to the allowed range before
mapping them to MW. A numeric zero denotes
minimum stable output, whereas off and missing
entries denote zero output. The final swing-unit
relaxation also permits positive output below its
minimum stable level in the hourly relaxation.
Task checks and satisfaction accounting are sep-
arate. Capacity and data-center power violations
are recorded per location and hour; the available
grid-aware satisfaction path excludes task-specific
violations and unpowered hours, but does not auto-
matically assign every location-hour violation to all
affected tasks. The archived placement-only path
omits both filters. Consequently, neither placement
satisfaction nor low aggregate violation certifies
that every task and every intertemporal constraint is
satisfied throughout the complete scheduling hori-
zon.
E
Baseline Detail
This appendix expands the experimental setup into
the model families behind Tables 1–3. Each fam-
ily is described by its overview, implementation,
and available hyperparameters. The shared inter-
face is followed by frontier models, open-weight
backbones, and PowerAtlas with its ablations.
Shared harness.
The evaluation uses a common
interface in three respects. (i) Output schema: all
systems receive the same serialized instance and re-
turn TASKS/POWER blocks without solver calls or
repair.
(ii) Physical evaluation: schedules are
checked with the same hourly LP (Appendix D.3);
satisfaction conventions are detailed separately in
Appendix F.1. (iii) Interaction: all models answer
in one turn without retrieved examples. Base and
trained versions in Table 2 use the same inference
procedure and differ in policy weights. Serving
conditions and latency definitions are specified in
Appendix F.1.
E.1
Frontier Language Models
Overview.
The eight frontier baselines are GPT-
5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash/Pro,
Kimi-K2.6 fast/pro, and Qwen3.7-Plus/Max. They
provide zero-shot joint schedules through an
OpenAI-compatible API.
Implementation.
Every model receives the same
serialized instance and prompt template (Ap-
pendix A), answers in one turn, and returns
the shared TASKS/POWER schema without retrieval,
solver calls, or repair. Reported frontier rows av-
erage their stored runs on the same high-load in-
stance; repeat counts appear in Table 7.


--- Page 20 ---
Hyperparameters.
The reported interface spec-
ifies the same decoding settings for these calls.
Provider implementations and serving conditions
may differ; the retained reporting summary does
not establish identical internal reasoning budgets or
complete provider-specific sampling provenance.
E.2
Open-Weight Language Models
Overview.
The three backbones are Qwen3-4B,
Llama-3.2-3B, and Falcon3-3B (Yang et al., 2025;
Grattafiori et al., 2024; Technology Innovation In-
stitute, 2024).
Implementation.
Base and trained policies use
local serving and the same single-response infer-
ence procedure; the policy weights change between
them. Saved base outputs cover 10 Qwen3-4B, 12
Llama-3.2-3B, and 40 Falcon3-3B instances. Each
selected PowerAtlas checkpoint covers all 40 in-
stances of the reporting pool.
Hyperparameters.
Reported
inference
uses
greedy decoding with vLLM 0.8.4. Hardware and
training settings are recorded in Appendix C; sam-
ple coverage and satisfaction conventions are spec-
ified in Appendix F.1.
E.3
PowerAtlas and Its Ablations
Overview.
PowerAtlas trains each backbone with
supervised initialization and FA-GRPO, then gen-
erates a joint schedule in one response.
Implementation.
For each open-weight back-
bone, the base model and PowerAtlas use the
same inference interface.
PowerAtlas adds su-
pervised initialization followed by FA-GRPO; its
training settings appear in Appendix C. Table 3
reports archived Falcon stage comparisons, with
two supervised-output histories separated. With-
out initialization, alignment begins from the base
backbone; without alignment, evaluation uses the
supervised checkpoint. The selected checkpoints,
available output counts, and satisfaction conven-
tions are recorded in Appendix F.1. Main satisfac-
tion is now uniform; sample coverage and incom-
plete historical configuration provenance remain
explicit.
Hyperparameters.
Alignment runs for up to 60
steps with group size two. The reported check-
points use step 40 for Qwen3-4B and Falcon3-3B,
and step 20 for Llama-3.2-3B. The supervised-only
and alignment-without-initialization rows are de-
fined by the omitted stage, with their scoring con-
ventions explicitly retained in Table 7.
F
Experiment Detail
This appendix expands Section 6: each subsection
specifies the protocol and numerical values behind
the corresponding research question. Tables 8–13
expose the coordinates summarized by Figure 5, to-
gether with sample counts and scoring conventions.
No additional model generations are introduced.
F.1
Shared Protocol
Four reporting conventions specify the scope of
results in Section 6.
(i) Sample size.
Results
for the three untrained backbones and the three
PowerAtlas configurations are averaged over their
available outputs from the held-out pool.
The
open-weight rows of Table 1 average the stored
answers for each backbone over that pool. The
frontier rows average all stored runs for each
model on one shared high-penetration instance
(ECCS-RTS-m01d15-rho06-s10); no run is se-
lected or discarded. The number of stored runs
varies across models, and the rows report point
estimates without dispersion. The two blocks of
Table 1 do not form a paired comparison. On
the shared instance, the selected checkpoints yield
192.7, 216.8 and 449.2 MWh, supporting lower
violation for two of the three backbones on that
instance. (ii) Model selection. ECBench has only
training and test splits. We select the initialization
duration and aligned checkpoint—step 40 (20 for
Llama-3.2-3B)—by comparing checkpoints on the
same held-out pool used in the tables. The shipped
steps are listed in Appendix C, but the trained rows
are estimates from selected checkpoints rather than
blind test results. Independent validation is needed
for model selection. (iii) Incomplete answers. The
evaluator scores a generator or an hour missing
from an answer as offline rather than skipping it,
so a truncated dispatch is charged the lost load
it leaves behind. This is why the untrained rows
of Table 1 reach violations an order of magnitude
above any frontier model: the penalty is for load
left uncovered, not for the missing text.
(iv) Satisfaction and evaluator versions. All sat-
isfaction columns in Tables 1–3 use the grid-aware
convention: task-specific violations and hours with
system-wide lost load above 1 MW are excluded.
This proxy does not assign lost load to individual
data centers; cell-level capacity violations receive

Table 7 lists the sample scope and satisfaction
convention for each reported configuration. The
historical evaluation pool contains 40 instances:
five dates (January 15, April 15, July 15, July 28,
and October 15), four data-center load levels, and
seeds 9 and 10. Saved baseline outputs cover sub-
sets of this pool; the three selected PowerAtlas
checkpoints each cover all 40 instances. The nomi-
nal 400-instance test split is therefore not the per-

tions.
The reported inference protocol uses one autore-
gressive response without retrieval, solver calls, or
repair. Frontier models use remote APIs; open-
weight models use local serving. Latency compar-
isons therefore include these serving conditions.
Appendix D.3 details the constraint checks.
Numerical sources and aggregation.
The de-
scriptive landscape uses full available archives and
historical cost/latency. Table 2 uses paired subsets
and re-scored cost, so its coordinates are separate.
The temporal panel uses six cached 24-hour se-
ries for one instance. The stage, tier, stratum, and
paired panels use the same 200 records: 40 in-
stances at each of Base, SFT, GRPO-20, GRPO-40,
and GRPO-60. Means, quartiles, and differences
below are recomputed from those records before
rounding. Placement scores and training residuals
are kept separate from final grid-aware evaluation
throughout.
F.2
Main Results and Ablations (RQ1, RQ2)
Tables 1 and 2 report the frontier and backbone
comparisons; Table 3 compares archived training
stages on Falcon3-3B. The violation reductions
and penalized-cost improvements summarize the
stored outputs under the sample scopes above. The
frontier comparison on one shared instance and
the open-weight averages over the reporting pool
answer different questions.
Protocol.
The comparison uses the selected poli-
cies and stored outputs specified in Appendix F.1.
Table 8 makes every point of the landscape ex-
plicit; the ablation values are already reported in
Table 3. A stage-curve row is not substituted for a
final-evaluator ablation row.
Results.
The selected trained policies have lower
average final violation and penalized cost than their
corresponding base rows. The stage comparisons
use identical scoring but cannot isolate reward de-
sign from initialization history, training budget, or
retrieval.
F.3
Residual Constraint Violations (RQ3)
Protocol.
Table 9 reproduces the two temporal
series in Figure 5(b). The upper series sums hourly
lost-load, over-generation, and line-overload slacks.
The lower series counts retained tasks cumulatively
when a task-specific violation is recorded or an ex-
ecution hour first encounters system-wide lost load
above 1 MW. Voluntary drops are excluded from
this count. This time-resolved view complements
the pool-level summaries.
Results.
The table separates the time at which
grid slack occurs from the time at which task fail-
ures accumulate.
A flat cumulative curve may
coexist with grid slack, and a complete dispatch
may still leave demand uncovered. Figure 7 illus-
trates incomplete dispatch, supply deficits, capac-
ity overflow, and timing or migration violations;
Appendix F.8 supplies the stored answer excerpts.
Final-pool violation composition is summarized in
Section 6.4; the stage residuals in the following
subsection use a different scorer.
F.4
Feasibility-Aware Alignment and
Checkpoints (RQ2, RQ4)
Figure 5(c)–(f) uses a separate earlier Falcon3-
3B run, not the selected SFT-16/PowerAtlas out-
put archive. The violation axis reports the train-
ing scorer’s power-balance residual, whereas Ap-
pendix D.3 uses an hourly DC LP that re-optimizes
the swing unit. The resulting values can differ sub-
stantially. Satisfaction is placement-based, before
filtering tasks by power availability. These panels
describe training trends and checkpoint selection;
their absolute values should not be compared di-
rectly with Table 3.
Protocol.
Each stage contains the same 40 in-
stance identifiers. The satisfaction curve is the
arithmetic mean of placement-value satisfaction,
while the boxplot is the distribution of aggregate
training-side balance residuals. Table 10 reports
the quartiles and plotted whiskers as well as the
line coordinates.
Results.
Mean placement-value satisfaction rises
from 6.81% at Base to 91.63% after SFT and
reaches 93.85% at GRPO-40, before decreasing
to 91.45% at GRPO-60. The residual median de-
creases from 11,957.59 to 4,204.86 at GRPO-40.
These stage records use the training-side scorer. Ta-
ble 15 gives final scores for these exact outputs and
distinguishes the later SFT-16 archive.

F.6
Cost and Efficiency (RQ1)
Protocol.
Table 8 reports penalized scheduling
cost and observed decision latency for the same
model rows. Scheduling cost combines genera-
tion, migration, drop, and grid-slack penalties; it is
not the financial cost of calling an LLM. Frontier
latency includes remote API serving, whereas open-
weight latency uses local serving. The Gurobi ref-
erence has reported median/maximum solve times
of 16.8/148.1 seconds.
Results.
For the selected open-weight policies,
reported latency is 18.5–57.2 seconds, and cost is
lower than the corresponding base-model averages.
The remaining cost includes penalties for physi-
cal deficits, so cost improvement alone does not
certify feasibility. Different hardware and serving
paths prevent a matched-runtime comparison with
frontier APIs or the reference solver.
F.7
Robustness and Significance of the
Margin (RQ3, RQ4)
Protocol.
Table 12 groups the 40 instances by
four load levels and five dated seasonal scenarios.
Table 13 preserves every base/GRPO-40 pair in the
order used by Figure 5(f). The exploratory interval
resamples the 40 instance pairs 4,000 times with
NumPy’s default random generator seeded at zero
and takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the
mean residual reduction. This is an instance-paired
interval conditional on the archived pool, not a
correction for checkpoint selection or an estimate
across independent training runs.
Results.
The training-side balance residual im-
proves on 37 of the 40 paired instances. The mean
reduction is 6,886.21, with an exploratory 95%
interval of [5,663.48, 8,065.77] in the same hourly-
summed residual units. The interval is conditional
on the archived paired sample and concerns the
training residual. Its scope excludes generalization
to unseen conditions and statistical significance
for the final nodal LP metric; checkpoint selection
follows Appendix F.1.
Re-scoring and strict-output audit.
Archived
predictions are re-scored without new generation
or checkpoint selection. All main-table satisfac-
tion rates use the same grid-aware proxy.
For
paired gains, instance IDs are intersected within
each backbone before averaging; no outputs are
discarded according to their score. Cost evaluation
uses HiGHS 1.15.1 with one thread: each hourly
LP first minimizes total slack, then minimizes
swing output subject to slack staying within 10−8
of that optimum. Optimal status and constraint
residuals are checked. This tie-break removes arbi-
trary swing choices from cost accounting; it does
not optimize commitment costs across hours. The
source script, prediction hashes, per-instance scores
and paired IDs are retained in the evaluation audit.
Offline re-scoring is not an inference-latency mea-
surement.
A separate retained-output check requires ev-
ery task, all five controlled units, exactly 24 levels
per unit, and finite percentages in [0, 100], with-
out clipping or padding. Invalid outputs remain in
the denominator. For valid outputs, controlled-unit
ramping and minimum up/down inequalities are
checked against the saved oracle code, including
its initial-off convention. All controlled trajectories
with valid retained outputs violate at least one of
these inequalities for the three selected checkpoints.
The audit does not recover fixed-unit commitment
or certify swing-unit dynamics and system reserve.
No complete-system feasibility claim follows from
an hourly score.
Paired and stage evidence.
The paired final-
violation reductions occur on 10/10 Qwen, 12/12
Llama, and 40/40 Falcon instances. These are ret-
rospective descriptive counts. The historical pool
repeats two task seeds across date/load strata and
was used for checkpoint selection; no independent-
training confidence interval is inferred from those
counts. Table 15 applies the same final evaluator to
the output archives underlying the separate training-
diagnostic trajectory. SFT-16 and the selected Pow-
erAtlas output are shown separately, avoiding a
substitution of the earlier SFT archive for the later

initialization history. Historical checkpoint prove-
nance is incomplete, so this remains a stage com-

design.
Optimization controls.
Existing supplementary
fixed-background HiGHS runs use the same 40
instance IDs and report every attempted instance,
including failures. Their acceptance check covers
output validity, tasks and hourly DC slack, not full
unit commitment. The greedy variant also invokes
a dispatch MILP. Reported time includes schedule
construction and verification on the local CPU host;
it cannot be compared as a matched-speed experi-
ment against historical GPU/API generation. These
controls show that the LLM scores do not estab-
lish superiority to conventional optimization. All
available 20/40-second configurations are reported,
without selecting the best budget.
Remaining evidence requirements.
A separate
100-instance validation set with new task seeds
already exists, but original policy weights are un-
available and no new original-model validation or
blind-test outputs have been produced. Its feasible-


--- Page 26 ---

timed failures.

incumbent reference labels are not claimed to be
optimal. Historical scorer coefficients, retrieval
bonuses and sampling configurations cannot be
assigned to every checkpoint from the retained
logs. Independent model selection, multiple train-
ing seeds, held-out operating regimes, and budget-
matched ordinary-GRPO/reward/retrieval ablations
therefore remain open; constructing protocols does
not count as completing these experiments.
Further evaluation.
Four directions require fur-
ther study. Evaluation scale: evaluate all meth-
ods on the full test set with identical metrics and
independent validation for checkpoint selection.
Generalization: hold out complete months or data-
center load levels rather than only generator seeds,
since the current splits share operating regimes.
Baselines: compare matched retrieval settings and
include solvers with matched latency budgets. Op-
timization: study larger trajectory groups than the
current size of two and evaluate retrieval use within
the policy. These experiments are needed to estab-
lish robustness beyond the reported settings.
F.8
Case Study (RQ3)
Figure 9 reproduces four stored model outputs. The
instance is m01d15-rho06-s10, a winter scenario
with ρ = 6% and 37 tasks. Its Gurobi-optimal
cost is $2.05M. The examples include the same
3B backbone before and after PowerAtlas. Met-
rics here describe the individual outputs shown,
whereas Table 1 averages each model’s stored runs.
Task placements are summarized in the accompa-
nying text alongside the corresponding dispatch
outcomes.
DeepSeek-V4-Pro: a missing unit and insuffi-
cient dispatch.
The dispatch in Figure 9(a) fol-
lows the morning and evening load pattern and
places 35 of 37 tasks.
However, 221_CC_1 is
missing, and all remaining controlled units are of-
fline during hours 1–4 and 9–14. The swing unit
alone cannot cover demand, leaving 2,291.6 MWh
unserved. Grid-aware evaluation excludes tasks
scheduled during unpowered hours, so only 5.6%
of task value is served despite the high placement
count in the generated task assignments.
Qwen3.7-Max: excess generation and unmet
peak demand.
Figure 9(b) includes all five con-
trolled units, mostly near maximum output. Task-
count satisfaction is 70.3%, but the schedule pro-
duces 498.5 MWh of excess generation while leav-
ing 150.8 MWh unserved at the peak. The nearly
constant output fails to follow changing net load.
With four dropped tasks, total cost is 4.1× the opti-
mum for this shared evaluation instance.
Falcon3-3B untrained: an incomplete output.
The untrained backbone emits an empty dispatch
header and drops all 37 tasks (Figure 9(c)). With
the swing unit carrying the load alone, unserved en-
ergy reaches 12,737.5 MWh and cost reaches 57×
the optimum. This example illustrates the output-
format failure in Figure 7, Case 1. When every
rollout receives the same format penalty, group-
relative rewards provide no signal for improving
scheduling decisions.
Falcon3-3B + PowerAtlas: similarities to the
reference schedule.
After training, the same 3B
backbone provides all five unit schedules with frac-
tional set-points (Figure 9(d)). Like the reference in
panel (e), it keeps 218_CC_1 offline and shuts down
321_CC_1 at hours 23–24. However, 321_CC_1 is
already online at hour 1 and remains at minimum
stable output during hours 2–5; its rise at hour 6 is
an output increase, not a start-up. Three units run at
hour 1 when the reference leaves them offline, and
108.9 MWh of peak demand is unserved. Together
with three dropped tasks, these errors raise cost to
1.57× the optimum. The model generates a struc-
tured schedule in one response, but verification and
correction are still needed before operational use
under the coupled grid and task constraints.
Output completeness and physical feasibility.
The examples distinguish output completeness
from physical feasibility. A complete schedule may
still leave tasks without power. Placement-based
satisfaction therefore overstates delivered service in
the first two cases; grid-aware evaluation accounts
for this dependency (Appendix F.1).

G
Related Work
G.1
LLM-Based Scheduling and
Optimization
LLM-based optimization and scheduling com-
bine structured outputs with reasoning or external
tools (Abgaryan et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024;
Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023b; Schick et al.,
2023; Yao et al., 2023a; Shinn et al., 2023). Power-
system applications include scheduling and dis-
patch (Mongaillard et al., 2024; Mohammadi et al.,
2025; Bernier et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Jia
et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Sarwar et al.,
2025), security analysis (Ruan et al., 2024), bench-
marks (Zhou et al., 2024; Han et al., 2022), topol-
ogy modeling (Chen et al., 2025), and physical
verification (Jiang et al., 2026).
Retrieval provides domain context through
stored cases or structured knowledge (Luo et al.,
2024, 2025a,b, 2026). PowerAtlas uses a training-
only corpus and removes retrieval from reported in-
ference. Its supervised initialization and FA-GRPO
stages also relate to instruction alignment, pol-
icy optimization, and verifiable feedback (Ouyang
et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017; Lightman et al.,
2024; Guo et al., 2025). Here, the feedback acts
on generated task placements and power trajecto-
ries. The proofs in Appendix B describe algebraic
properties of this feedback and its evaluation scope,
while the experiments measure the remaining vio-
lations in generated schedules.
For comparing these approaches, the location of
verification in the workflow matters. A verifier that
scores training rollouts supplies a learning signal,
whereas one applied after generation measures the
returned decision. A solver invoked during infer-
ence can participate in constructing or correcting
that decision.
PowerAtlas uses executable training feedback
and a separate evaluator for reporting, while its in-
ference policy emits the schedule directly. Output
syntax, physical feasibility, and end-to-end com-


--- Page 28 ---
putational cost therefore need separate assessment
when comparing these decision-generation proce-
dures.
G.2
Grid-Constrained Co-Scheduling
Work on carbon-aware and power-flexible com-
puting studies how workload timing and location
affect energy use and operating cost (Radovanovi´c
et al., 2023; Wiesner et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2026;
Nkwawir et al., 2025). Grid signals and flexibility
models connect these scheduling choices to avail-
able power (Zhang et al., 2022; Williams et al.,
2026). More detailed formulations incorporate hi-
erarchical control, spatial placement, thermal be-
havior, and multi-energy coordination (Han et al.,
2024; Su et al., 2025; Ali and Özkasap, 2024;
Liu, 2024; Bian et al., 2024), with optimization
and reinforcement learning among the solution ap-
proaches (Luo et al., 2025c; Qi et al., 2022).
ECBench adopts this coupled decision setting:
placing tasks changes nodal demand, while genera-
tor dispatch and network limits constrain service.
Its contribution is a structured generation task with
solved references and executable checks. The dis-
tinction between the full optimization model and
the evaluator’s constraint coverage is explicit in
Appendices D.1 and D.3; learned schedules are not
assumed to inherit the oracle’s feasibility proper-
ties.
